questions.stem:
For a new branch bank, the owner furnished a boundary and topographic survey prepared by its surveyor. During a site visit early in schematic design, the project architect notices that a large existing storm inlet near the entrance isn't on the survey, and the curb elevations there look about two feet different from the survey's spot grades.

What should the architect do?

options.text: Correct the survey on the architect's base drawings
options.explanation: The architect shouldn't revise the owner's consultant's work.

options.text: Notify the owner in writing of the inconsistency
options.explanation: Correct. The architect may rely on the survey but must give prompt written notice of errors it becomes aware of.

options.text: Keep relying on the survey, as the agreement permits
options.explanation: The right to rely ends when the architect becomes aware of an error.

options.text: Hire a second surveyor and bill the owner
options.explanation: Surveys are the owner's responsibility, and the owner must agree to more services.

questions.explanation: Reliance on owner information ends at awareness of an error. Notify the owner in writing.
questions.confidenceNote: Paragraph number per my knowledge of the AIA document; confirm against your copy (free via your NCARB Record).

questions.stem:
The owner of a hotel has hired its own food-service consultant and audiovisual consultant. The owner now wants the architect to incorporate their drawings into the construction documents, run their coordination meetings and track their deliverables. The architect's B101 doesn't list coordination of owner's consultants as a supplemental service.

How should the architect handle the request?

options.text: Provide the coordination within basic services
options.explanation: Coordinating the owner's consultants beyond the architect's own coordination is a supplemental or additional service.

options.text: Propose it as an additional service
options.explanation: Correct. Because it isn't in the agreement, the architect proposes it as an additional service.

options.text: Refuse to include their work in the documents
options.explanation: The architect must still coordinate its own services with theirs.

options.text: Have the consultants sign C401s with the architect
options.explanation: Changing who contracts with the consultants is a bigger change than the owner asked for.

questions.explanation: Coordinating owner's consultants is a supplemental service. If it isn't listed, it's additional.
questions.confidenceNote: Paragraph number per my knowledge of the AIA document; confirm against your copy (free via your NCARB Record).

questions.stem:
At 95% construction documents for a laboratory, the owner's commissioning agent issues comments based on the owner's project requirements. Several comments ask for redundant exhaust fans and a different control strategy than the MEP design the owner approved at DD. The changes would add about $180,000 and three weeks.

What should the architect do?

options.text: Incorporate every comment before issuing the construction documents
options.explanation: Changes from the approved DD that affect cost and schedule need the owner's decision.

options.text: Review them with the MEP engineer and refer cost items to the owner
options.explanation: Correct. Respond in writing, and let the owner decide on changes that affect cost and schedule.

options.text: Disregard the comments because DD was approved
options.explanation: Commissioning comments may reveal real conflicts with the owner's requirements.

options.text: Ask the contractor to price the comments during bidding
options.explanation: Deciding during bidding is too late and creates uncertainty in the bids.

questions.explanation: Commissioning comments: review them with consultants, respond in writing, and refer cost and schedule changes to the owner.

questions.stem:
A biotech owner has hired a lab-planning consultant to design the casework, fume hoods and lab gas layouts. To save effort, the owner asks the architect to put the lab planner's drawings in the construction documents under the architect's seal. The architect hasn't directed or supervised the lab planner's work.

How should the architect respond?

options.text: Seal the drawings after a detailed review
options.explanation: A review after the fact isn't responsible control.

options.text: Coordinate them into the set without sealing them
options.explanation: Correct. The architect can coordinate them into the set but seals only what it prepared or controlled.

options.text: Redraw the lab drawings so the architect can seal them
options.explanation: Redrawing duplicates the owner's consultant's work and takes on its responsibility.

options.text: Seal them if the owner signs an indemnity
options.explanation: An indemnity doesn't satisfy responsible control.

questions.explanation: Seal only work prepared under your responsible control (NCARB 5.1).

questions.stem:
For a university building, the owner will hire separate contractors for telecommunications cabling and for movable furniture, both installed during the general contractor's work. The architect is planning its CA services and staffing. The owner asks who will coordinate these separate contractors with the general contractor.

What should the architect tell the owner?

options.text: The architect coordinates them within basic CA services
options.explanation: Coordinating the owner's separate contractors is the owner's duty under A201.

options.text: The owner coordinates them with the architect's help
options.explanation: Correct. A201 Art. 6 makes the owner responsible for coordinating its separate contractors.

options.text: The general contractor coordinates them automatically
options.explanation: The contractor cooperates, but coordination belongs to the owner unless the contract assigns it.

options.text: Each separate contractor coordinates itself
options.explanation: Someone must coordinate. A201 assigns it to the owner.

questions.explanation: The owner coordinates its separate contractors (A201 Art. 6).
questions.confidenceNote: Paragraph number per my knowledge of the AIA document; confirm against your copy (free via your NCARB Record).

questions.stem:
The owner of a corporate headquarters has hired a security consultant to design access control and cameras. At the kickoff, the architect is concerned that nobody has said who will design the conduit, the backboxes and the door hardware wiring for the security devices, which caused change orders on a past project.

What should the architect request first?

options.text: The security consultant's scope of services
options.explanation: Correct. Comparing the owner's consultant's scope with the architect's team shows the gaps to assign.

options.text: The security consultant's insurance certificates
options.explanation: Insurance is for the owner to require. It doesn't define who designs what.

options.text: A fee proposal to design the security systems
options.explanation: Taking over the consultant's work isn't the first step.

options.text: The contractor's security subcontractor list
options.explanation: There's no contractor yet, and design scope comes first.

questions.explanation: Get the owner's consultants' scopes early and assign the gaps.
questions.confidenceNote: B101 Art. 5 lets the architect request owner-consultant scopes; confirm paragraph.

questions.stem:
The owner's equipment planner for a hospital was due to deliver the imaging-equipment requirements at the start of design development. It's now four weeks late, and the architect's team can't finish the imaging suite's structural and MEP design without the data. The approved schedule included the planner's delivery date.

What should the architect do?

options.text: Design using assumed equipment and revise later
options.explanation: Designing on assumptions risks rework the owner hasn't approved.

options.text: Notify the owner in writing and update the schedule
options.explanation: Correct. The owner is responsible for its consultant's timing. The owner needs to see the effect, and the record supports any additional services.

options.text: Contact the equipment manufacturer for the data directly
options.explanation: Getting the owner's consultant's information is the owner's job.

options.text: Remove the imaging suite from the DD submission
options.explanation: Dropping the scope without the owner's decision isn't appropriate.

questions.explanation: Late owner's consultants: notify the owner in writing and update the schedule.

questions.stem:
For the renovation of a 1960s school, the owner furnished a hazardous-materials survey from its consultant. The survey excluded the crawl space because it wasn't accessible. During a later site visit, the architect's staff sees pipe insulation in the crawl space that looks like it may contain asbestos.

What should the architect do?

options.text: Specify asbestos abatement for the crawl space
options.explanation: Without testing, the architect would be taking on hazardous-materials responsibility the agreement excludes.

options.text: Notify the owner in writing and recommend testing
options.explanation: Correct. The owner is responsible for testing. The architect has no responsibility for discovering or removing hazardous materials.

options.text: Take a sample for the owner's laboratory
options.explanation: Sampling suspected asbestos is for qualified consultants.

options.text: Note it for the contractor to investigate during construction
options.explanation: Leaving it until construction risks exposure, delay and a change order.

questions.explanation: Suspected hazardous materials: notify the owner in writing. Testing is the owner's responsibility.
